# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" (statutory term, 8 U.S.C. 1365) in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. The series argues for stronger interior enforcement; copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and date. Population, timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Prefer federal primary sources (ICE, USSC, GAO, BJS) over secondary analyses.
B3. Counter-research (e.g. Cato's Texas DPS analyses): appendix only, one line, followed by CIS's methodological critique.
B4. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers' - FactCheck.org

 This article is available in both English and Español

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

 Mittelstadt said some murderers and other criminals cannot be deported “because their country will not accept their return.” In addition, she said, a 2001 Supreme Court ruling generally bars ICE from detaining noncitizens for more than six months if they are unlikely to be deported. As a result, ICE says on its website that it “has been legally required to release thousands of noncitizens, including those with serious criminal convictions.”

John Moore / Getty Images file Share Add NBC News to Google Sept. 28, 2024, 9:30 AM EDT  /  Updated   Sept. 28, 2024, 3:50 PM EDT By Julia Ainsley , Laura Strickler and Gabe Gutierrez More than 13,000 immigrants convicted of homicide — either in the United States or abroad — are living outside of Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention, according to data ICE provided to Congress earlier this week.
 The immigrants are part of ICE’s “non-detained” docket, meaning the agency has some information on the immigrants and they have pending immigration cases in the U.S., but they are not currently in detention either because they are not prioritized for detention, they are serving time in a jail or prison for their crimes, or because ICE cannot find them, three law enforcement officials said.
 Two of the officials said it is not known how many are incarcerated because ICE is not always privy to that data from state and local law enforcement agencies.
 Acting ICE Director P.J. Lechleitner sent the data, collected as of July 21, as part of a request sent in March from Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales of Texas.
 A spokesman for the Department of Homeland Security said the data sent to Gonzales is being misinterpreted, and goes back four decades, long before the Biden administration.

 Harris makes first trip to U.S. southern border in three years 02:25 It is not clear when the first migrant of the 13,000 crossed into the U.S.   Two law enforcement officials familiar with the data told NBC News many of the migrants on ICE’s non-detained docket, including serious criminals, crossed into the U.S. under previous administrations, including that of former President Donald Trump .
 A high number of non-detained immigrants with criminal convictions is not new, though it has grown in recent years.
 A 2016 DHS Inspector General's report found there were 368,000 criminal immigrants who were not detained by ICE. According to ICE's fiscal year 2023 budget justification, there were 405,786 convicted criminal immigrants on the non-detained docket as of June 5, 2021, just under five months after Trump left office, indicating many crossed during the Trump administration. As of July of this year, according to the data provided by ICE to Rep. Gonzales, over 435,719 convicted criminal immigrants were on ICE's non-detained docket. 
 A DHS spokesman told NBC News in a statement: "The data in this letter is being misinterpreted. The data goes back decades; it includes people who entered the country over the past 40 year or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this administration. It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners."

 “I can finally look at them and say ‘I told you so’ to the fake news,” Trump  said. “These are hard, tough, vicious criminals that are free to roam in our country.”
 The White House has yet to comment on the data. One official told NBC News the release of the data came as a surprise to the White House.

Trump makes misleading claim about migrants with criminal records Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Migrants with criminal records - what new US data shows
 2 October 2024 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jake Horton & Lucy Gilder BBC Verify Getty Images Newly-released figures about migrants with criminal convictions are being used to attack Democrats for the border policies under President Biden and Kamala Harris. 
 Donald Trump has used the figures to claim that "13,000 convicted murderers entered our country during her three and a half year period as Border Czar" and said they were allowed to "openly roam our country".
 But both claims are misleading.
 The new figures released by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) do show some 13,000 non-citizens convicted of homicide were on its records and not in its custody.
 However, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said the figures cover a period of many years, and include migrants who entered the US under the Trump presidency and previous administrations.
 It also said that those on the list may not be in ICE custody but could be detained or in prison under the supervision of other agencies.
 What do the figures show? 
 The figures were released in a letter from ICE to Republican congressman Tony Gonzales, who had requested them. 
 They show that, as of July 2024, there were 425,431 non-citizens with criminal convictions on ICE’s "non-detained docket" - a database of people facing deportation proceedings but who are not held in ICE custody.
 Of these: 
 13,099 were convicted of homicide
 15,811 were convicted of sexual assault
 62,231 were convicted of assault
 However, a DHS statement said the data had been “misinterpreted". 
 “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners,” the DHS said.
 So, just because they are not being held by ICE, it does not mean they are all "roaming freely", as Trump claims. 
 “For example, Zacarias Moussaoui, who’s in a maximum security prison in Colorado for his role in the 9/11 attacks, is not currently detained by ICE so will likely be on that list,” says Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
 BBC Verify has asked the DHS how many are being held in detention by other agencies. 
 How many of them came under Biden and Harris?
 Trump said that the 13,000 convicted of killing someone entered the US under the Biden-Harris administration, but the ICE figures do not state when these people came to America.
 The DHS said: "The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this [Biden-Harris] administration."
 The non-detained docket is not routinely released and it is only published under certain circumstances on request - so we do not have exact numbers under each administration.
 The numbers were previously published in June 2021 , five months into the Biden presidency, which showed there were 405,431 convicted criminals on the list at that time.
 Before that, an official report published in August 2016 , towards the end of Barack Obama's presidency, showed 368,574.
 So, the list grew by almost 37,000 over five years, which includes Trump’s term in office.
 “This data shows a significant number would have gotten on the list during the prior administrations, and the docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one,” said Michelle Mittelstadt of the Migration Policy Institute.
 The overall number of non-citizens on the list has increased in recent years due to high levels of immigration under President Biden. 
 “Although, the number of people on the non-detained docket has increased substantially under the Biden administration, the number of people who are convicted criminals on the list hasn’t,” says Mr Reichlin-Melnick.
 In the letter, ICE does not specify how many of the non-citizens with criminal convictions on its list are illegal immigrants and how many entered the US with, for example, a green card.
 BBC Verify has asked for a breakdown.
 How many migrants have crossed the US border illegally?
 Why is it difficult to remove some criminals from the US?
 Part of the reason why overall numbers are high, experts say, is because of problems with deporting certain non-citizens who have committed crimes.
 “The US government cannot put a person on a commercial or government flight to return them to their country of nationality without agreement by that country,” says Michelle Mittelstadt.

A convicted killer finishing a state sentence walks out the prison gate into the country unless a detainer is honored. A convicted killer already in the community is a federal warrant that has not been served.

The docket has grown under administrations of both parties: 368,574 convicted criminals as of August 2016, 405,786 as of June 2021 and 425,431 as of July 2024, about 15% more than eight years ago. The federal courts quantify the flow. In fiscal 2024, the U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentenced cases, and 21,304 involved noncitizens, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens; another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

A September 2024 GAO review found the same pattern across a longer window: about three-quarters of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023, 76%, had an immigration offense as their most serious conviction.

Texas is the one state that records immigration status in its criminal conviction files, which makes the Texas Department of Public Safety the country's best available record of how often illegal aliens are convicted of crimes. An analysis of those conviction records by the Center for Immigration Studies concludes that illegal aliens are convicted of crimes in Texas at higher rates than native-born Americans, because prior studies counted illegal aliens identified at intake but missed illegal aliens identified as such only after incarceration.

The state data carry two lessons for Congress. First, the only routine window into alien offending is one state's bookkeeping, which is why DHS should be required to publish its own. Second, every argument that illegal alien crime is trivial rests on denominators that understate the population. When Congress legislates on the strength of crime-rate claims, it should demand the underlying records, not the summary.

Interior enforcement fails at a single, identifiable point: the transfer of custody. In November 2024 an Athens judge convicted him of Riley's murder and sentenced him to life without parole.

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention capacity and direct ICE to take custody of every noncitizen on the non-detained docket convicted of homicide or a violent felony the day other custody ends.
2. **Condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance.** Require state and local grantees to honor ICE detainers and comply with 8 U.S.C. 1373, and withhold discretionary funds from agencies ICE lists as noncompliant.
3. **Expand Section 287(g) nationwide.** Fund new delegation agreements in every state, prioritizing jurisdictions where detainers are declined and criminal aliens are released.
4. **Publish the docket.** Require DHS to report quarterly on the size of the non-detained docket, releases by criminal category, and every declined detainer, by agency.

The federal government already knows who these offenders are; it compiled the docket. What it has not done is take custody, require cooperation or publish the numbers until Congress makes it. The data in this brief are the government's own. The choice about what to do with them belongs to Congress.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories as of July 21, 2024. The non-detained docket alone held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, plus another 222,141 awaiting criminal charges.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- From October 2020 through July 2024, state and local agencies declined 23,591 ICE detainers, and in 2,897 of those cases ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

On Sept. 25, 2024, acting ICE Director Patrick J. Lechleitner answered a request from Rep. Tony Gonzales with the numbers no briefing book could soften. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. Of those, 425,431 convicted criminals were on the non-detained docket, the ledger of cases in which ICE holds no one.

The offense categories are the point. The non-detained docket that day included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault. Another 222,141 people on the same docket were awaiting criminal charges, 1,845 of them on murder charges.

These are adjudicated convictions in the files of the agency Congress charges with removing criminal aliens from the United States. They are not projections, and they are not news analysis. ICE did not report how many of the 13,099 are finishing sentences in state or county custody and how many are already in the community. Either answer indicts the status quo. A convicted killer finishing a state sentence walks out the prison gate into the country unless a detainer is honored. A convicted killer already in the community is a federal warrant that has not been served.

The docket has grown under administrations of both parties: 368,574 convicted criminals as of August 2016, 405,786 as of June 2021 and 425,431 as of July 2024, about 15% more than eight years ago. What stands between the docket and the public is bed space Congress funds and local cooperation Congress has not required.

Hmm, that last sentence is good.

## 2. One in Three Federal Sentences

The federal courts quantify the flow. In fiscal 2024, the U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentenced cases, and 21,304 involved noncitizens, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens; another 8.5% were legal aliens whose convictions made them removable.

The immigration guideline was the most common basis for a noncitizen sentence, 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%. A September 2024 GAO review found the same pattern across a longer window: about three-quarters of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023, 76%, had an immigration offense as their most serious conviction.

Federal figures are a floor, not a ceiling. Homicide, rape, robbery and assault are prosecuted overwhelmingly in state courts, and a noncitizen convicted in a state courthouse never appears in the Sentencing Commission's files. The federal data that do exist describe a criminal-alien casework load the government already cannot finish.

## 3. Texas Puts a Number on It

Texas is the one state that records immigration status in its criminal conviction files, which makes the Texas Department of Public Safety the country's best available record of how often illegal aliens are convicted of crimes. An analysis of those conviction records by the Center for Immigration Studies concludes that illegal aliens are convicted of crimes in Texas at higher rates than native-born Americans, because prior studies counted illegal aliens identified at intake but missed illegal aliens identified as such only after incarceration.

The state data carry two lessons for Congress. First, the only routine window into alien offending is one state's bookkeeping, which is why DHS should be required to publish its own. Second, every argument that illegal alien crime is trivial rests on denominators that understate the population. When Congress legislates on the strength of crime-rate claims, it should demand the underlying records, not the summary.

## 4. The Detainer Problem: 23,591 Refusals

Interior enforcement fails at a single, identifiable point: the transfer of custody. ICE's letter to Congress describes "refusal to honor ICE detainer requests, even for noncitizens who have been convicted of serious felonies and pose an ongoing threat to public safety." From October 2020 through July 22, 2024, state and local agencies declined 23,591 detainers, and 1,205 more were lifted because ICE received insufficient notice. In 2,897 declined cases, ERO later re-apprehended the same subject. ICE's own Detainer Acceptance Tracker, current as of June 21, 2024, lists 551 institutions that do not accept immigration detainers at all and another 146 that accept them only in limited fashion.

The cost of refusal is not hypothetical. On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, was killed while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Jose Ibarra, a 26-year-old Venezuelan national, had entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and been released pending his immigration case. He was arrested in New York in August 2023 on a child endangerment charge and released before ICE could file a detainer. He was also wanted in Georgia for missing a court date in a shoplifting case. In November 2024 an Athens judge convicted him of Riley's murder and sentenced him to life without parole.

Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1, signed Jan. 29, 2025), which requires DHS to take into custody aliens charged with theft. The law closed one gap. Detainer compliance, bed space and public reporting close the rest.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention capacity and direct ICE to take custody of every noncitizen on the non-detained docket convicted of homicide or a violent felony the day other custody ends.
2. **Condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance.** Require state and local grantees to honor ICE detainers and comply with 8 U.S.C. 1373, and withhold discretionary funds from agencies ICE lists as noncompliant.
3. **Expand Section 287(g) nationwide.** Fund new delegation agreements in every state, prioritizing jurisdictions where detainers are declined and criminal aliens are released.
4. **Publish the docket.** Require DHS to report quarterly on the size of the non-detained docket, releases by criminal category, and every declined detainer, by agency.

The federal government already knows who these offenders are; it compiled the docket. What it has not done is take custody, require cooperation or publish the numbers until Congress makes it. The data in this brief are the government's own. The choice about what to do with them belongs to Congress.

{"path": "/workspace/out/brief.md", "content": "# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | Draft for editorial review; copy deadline Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories as of July 21, 2024. The non-detained docket alone held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, plus another 222,141 awaiting criminal charges.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- From October 2020 through July 2024, state and local law enforcement agencies declined 23,591 ICE detainers, and in 2,897 of those cases ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

On Sept. 25, 2024, then-acting ICE Director Patrick J. Lechleitner answered a request from Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, with numbers no briefing book could soften. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. Of those, 425,431 convicted criminals sat on the non-detained docket, the ledger of cases in which ICE holds no one.

The offense categories are the point. The non-detained docket that day included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault. Another 222,141 people on the same docket were awaiting criminal charges, 1,845 of them on murder charges.

These are adjudicated criminal convictions in the files of the agency Congress charges with removing criminal aliens from the United States. They are not projections, and they are not advocacy. ICE did not report how many of the 13,099 are finishing sentences in state or county custody and how many are already in the community. Either answer indicts the status quo. A convicted killer finishing a state sentence walks out the prison gate into the country unless a federal detainer is honored. A convicted killer already in the community is a federal warrant that has not been served.

The docket has grown under administrations of both parties: 368,574 convicted criminals as of August 2016, 405,786 as of June 2021 and 425,431 as of July 2024, roughly 15% more in eight years. What stands between that docket and the public is bed space Congress funds and local cooperation Congress has never required.

## 2. One in Three Federal Sentences

The federal courts quantify the flow. In fiscal 2024 the U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentenced cases, and 21,304 of them involved noncitizens, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens; another 8.5% were legal aliens.

The immigration guideline was the most common basis for a noncitizen sentence, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%. A September 2024 GAO review found the same pattern over a longer window: about three-quarters of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023, 76%, had an immigration offense as their most serious conviction.

Federal figures are a floor, not a ceiling. Homicide, rape, robbery and assault are prosecuted overwhelmingly in state courts, and a noncitizen convicted in a state courthouse never appears in the Sentencing Commission's files. The federal data that do exist describe a criminal-alien caseload the government already cannot finish.

## 3. Texas Puts a Number on It

Texas is the one state that records immigration status in its criminal conviction files, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety records the country's best available record of how often illegal aliens are convicted of crimes. An analysis of those conviction records by the Center for Immigration Studies concludes that illegal aliens are convicted of crimes in Texas at higher rates than native-born Americans, because prior studies counted only illegal aliens identified at intake and missed illegal aliens identified as such only after incarceration.

The state data carry two lessons for Congress. First, the only routine window into alien offending is a single state's bookkeeping, which is why DHS should be required to publish its own numbers. Second, every claim that illegal-alien crime is trivial rests on denominators that understate the offending population. When Congress legislates on the strength of crime-rate claims, it should demand the underlying records, not the summary.

## 4. The Detainer Problem: 23,591 Refusals

Interior enforcement fails at a single, identifiable point: the transfer of custody. ICE's own letter to Congress describes jurisdictions that refuse to honor "ICE detainer requests, even for noncitizens who have been convicted of serious felonies and pose an ongoing threat to public safety." From Oct. 1, 2020, through July 22, 2024, state and local agencies declined 23,591 detainers, and another 1,205 were lifted because ICE received insufficient notice. In 2,897 declined cases, ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject. ICE's Detainer Acceptance Tracker, current as of June 21, 2024, lists 551 institutions that do not accept immigration detainers at all and another 146 that accept them only in limited fashion.

The cost of refusal is not hypothetical. On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, was killed while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Jose Ibarra, a 26-year-old Venezuelan national, had entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and been released pending his immigration case. He was arrested in New York in August 2023 on a child endangerment charge and released before ICE could file a detainer, and he was wanted in Georgia for missing a court date in a shoplifting case. In November 2024 an Athens judge convicted him of Riley's murder and sentenced him to life without parole.

Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1, signed Jan. 29, 2025), which requires the Department of Homeland Security to take into custody aliens charged with theft. The law closed one gap. Detainer compliance, bed space and public reporting close the rest.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention capacity, and direct ICE to take custody of every noncitizen on the non-detained docket convicted of homicide or a violent felony on the day other custody ends.
2. **Condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance.** Require state and local grantees to honor ICE detainers and comply with 8 U.S.C. 1373, and withhold discretionary funds from agencies ICE lists as noncompliant.
3. **Expand Section 287(g) nationwide.** Fund new delegation agreements in every state, prioritizing jurisdictions where detainers are declined and criminal aliens are released.
4. **Publish the docket.** Require DHS to report quarterly on the size of the non-detained docket, releases by criminal category and every declined detainer, by agency.

The federal government already knows who these offenders are; it compiled the docket. What it has not done is take custody, require cooperation and publish the numbers until Congress makes it. The data in this brief are the government's own. The choice about what to do with them belongs to Congress.

*Data appendix and sourcing for every figure in this brief: "Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, Data Appendix," Founders' Square Institute, October 2026.*"}

# Press Release | Founders' Square Institute

**EMBARGOED UNTIL TUESDAY, OCT. 27, 2026, 10:00 A.M. ET**

Contact: Office of Communications, Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.

## FSI Brief: 13,099 Noncitizens Convicted of Homicide Sit on ICE's Non-Detained Docket

**"Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show" urges Congress to fund custody, require detainer compliance and publish the docket**

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026: The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy Brett Kessler.

Drawing on ICE's Sept. 25, 2024, letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, the brief reports that ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories as of July 21, 2024. The non-detained docket alone held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault, with another 222,141 awaiting criminal charges.

Federal sentencing records point the same way. Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.

The brief also documents 23,591 detainers declined by state and local agencies between October 2020 and July 2024, 2,897 of them cases in which ICE later re-apprehended the same subject, and closes with the case of Laken Riley, the Augusta University nursing student killed in Athens, Georgia, in February 2024.

"Every number in this brief is the federal government's own," Kessler said. "ICE counted 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide on a docket of cases it does not hold, and the Sentencing Commission found that one in three people sentenced in federal court last fiscal year was a noncitizen. Congress does not need more anecdotes to act on interior enforcement. It needs to fund custody, require detainer compliance and publish the docket."

The brief recommends four steps for Congress: fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance, expand Section 287(g) agreements and require quarterly public DHS reporting.

Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices are available from the institute. Kessler is available for interviews.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | Draft for editorial review; copy deadline Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories as of July 21, 2024. The non-detained docket alone held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, plus another 222,141 awaiting criminal charges.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- From October 2020 through July 2024, state and local law enforcement agencies declined 23,591 ICE detainers, and in 2,897 of those cases ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

On Sept. 25, 2024, then-acting ICE Director Patrick J. Lechleitner answered a request from Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, with numbers no briefing book could soften. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. Of those, 425,431 convicted criminals sat on the non-detained docket, the ledger of cases in which ICE holds no one.

How should the country size the public-safety cost of illegal immigration? Begin with the question no agency has volunteered to answer: of the people on the federal government's immigration ledger, how many have killed someone? ICE's answer of July 21, 2024, was 13,099 for homicide convictions alone, and the offense list runs on from there.

The offense categories are the point. The non-detained docket that day included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault. Another 222,141 people on the same docket were awaiting criminal charges, 1,845 of them on murder charges.

These are adjudicated criminal convictions in the files of the agency Congress charges with removing criminal aliens from the United States. They are not projections, and they are not advocacy. ICE did not report how many of the 13,099 are finishing sentences in state or county custody and how many are already in the community. Either answer indicts the status quo. A convicted killer finishing a state sentence walks out the prison gate into the country unless a federal detainer is honored. A convicted killer already in the community is a federal warrant that has not been served.

The docket has grown under administrations of both parties: 368,574 convicted criminals as of August 2016, 405,786 as of June 2021 and 425,431 as of July 2024, roughly 15% more in eight years. What stands between t
... [2641 chars truncated] ...
em: 23,591 Refusals

Interior enforcement fails at a single, identifiable point: the transfer of custody. ICE's own letter to Congress describes jurisdictions that refuse to honor "ICE detainer requests, even for noncitizens who have been convicted of serious felonies and pose an ongoing threat to public safety." From Oct. 1, 2020, through July 22, 2024, state and local agencies declined 23,591 detainers, and another 1,205 were lifted because ICE received insufficient notice. In 2,897 declined cases, ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject. ICE's Detainer Acceptance Tracker, current as of June 21, 2024, lists 551 institutions that do not accept immigration detainers at all and another 146 that accept them only in limited fashion.

The cost of refusal is not hypothetical. On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, was killed while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Jose Ibarra, a 26-year-old Venezuelan national, had entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and been released pending his immigration case. He was arrested in New York in August 2023 on a child endangerment charge and released before ICE could file a detainer, and he was wanted in Georgia for missing a court date in a shoplifting case. In November 2024 an Athens judge convicted him of Riley's murder and sentenced him to life without parole.

Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1, signed Jan. 29, 2025), which requires the Department of Homeland Security to take into custody aliens charged with theft. The law closed one gap. Detainer compliance, bed space and public reporting close the rest.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention capacity, and direct ICE to take custody of every noncitizen on the non-detained docket convicted of homicide or a violent felony on the day other custody ends.
2. **Condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance.** Require state and local grantees to honor ICE detainers and comply with 8 U.S.C. 1373, and withhold discretionary funds from agencies ICE lists as noncompliant.
3. **Expand Section 287(g) nationwide.** Fund new delegation agreements in every state, prioritizing jurisdictions where detainers are declined and criminal aliens are released.
4. **Publish the docket.** Require DHS to report quarterly on the size of the non-detained docket, releases by criminal category and every declined detainer, by agency.

The federal government already knows who these offenders are; it compiled the docket. What it has not done is take custody, require cooperation and publish the numbers until Congress makes it. The data in this brief are the government's own. The choice about what to do with them belongs to Congress.

## 2. One in Three Federal Sentences

The federal courts quantify the flow. In fiscal 2024 the U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentenced cases, and 21,304 of them involved noncitizens, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens; another 8.5% were legal aliens.

The immigration guideline was the most common basis for a noncitizen sentence, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%. A September 2024 GAO review found the same pattern over a longer window: about three-quarters of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023, 76%, had an immigration offense as their most serious conviction.

Nor is the caseload an abstraction. The Sentencing Commission's profile of the fiscal 2024 noncitizen defendant: 94.4% men, an average age of 38, and 65.9% Mexican nationals, followed by Honduras at 8.7% and Guatemala at 5.8%.

Federal figures are a floor, not a ceiling. Homicide, rape, robbery and assault are prosecuted overwhelmingly in state courts, and a noncitizen convicted in a state courthouse never appears in the Sentencing Commission's files. The federal data that do exist describe a criminal-alien caseload the government already cannot finish.

## 3. Texas Puts a Number on It

Texas is the one state that records immigration status in its criminal conviction files, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety records the country's best available record of how often illegal aliens are convicted of crimes. An analysis of those conviction records by the Center for Immigration Studies concludes that illegal aliens are convicted of crimes in Texas at higher rates than native-born Americans, because prior studies counted only illegal aliens identified at intake and missed illegal aliens identified as such only after incarceration.

No other state keeps these records. For the other 49, neither Congress nor DHS can say how many of a state's convicts are illegal aliens, which is reason enough to write the reporting requirement into federal law.

The state data carry two lessons for Congress. First, the only routine window into alien offending is a single state's bookkeeping, which is why DHS should be required to publish its own numbers. Second, every claim that illegal-alien crime is trivial rests on denominators that understate the offending population. When Congress legislates on the strength of crime-rate claims, it should demand the underlying records, not the summary.

## 4. The Detainer Problem: 23,591 Refusals

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14: Fact Sheet

**Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show**
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Draft for editorial review | Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Key statistics

**1. 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide sat on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.** Another 15,811 on the same docket were convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 of assault. [1]

**2. 425,431 convicted criminals in all were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.** The national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories, and another 222,141 on the non-detained docket were awaiting criminal charges. [1]

**3. Noncitizens were 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024: 21,304 of the 61,678 cases reported.** [2]

**4. 88.7% of those sentenced noncitizens were illegal aliens.** Another 8.5% were legal aliens. [2]

**5. 72.3% of noncitizen federal sentences in fiscal 2024 were under the immigration guideline.** Drug trafficking was next at 17.6%. Across fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, 76% of federally sentenced noncitizens had an immigration offense as their most serious conviction. [2][3]

**6. State and local agencies declined 23,591 ICE detainers between Oct. 1, 2020, and July 22, 2024.** In 2,897 of those cases ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject. [1]

**7. 551 institutions refuse ICE detainers outright.** Another 146 accept detainers only in limited fashion, under ICE's own Detainer Acceptance Tracker, as of June 21, 2024. [4]

**8. The convicted-criminal non-detained docket grew from 368,574 in August 2016 to 425,431 in July 2024, about 15%.** It passed 405,786 in June 2021. [1][5][6]

## What Congress should do

1. Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, with mandatory ICE custody for homicide and violent-felony convictions at the end of other custody.
2. Condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance and compliance with 8 U.S.C. 1373.
3. Expand Section 287(g) agreements nationwide.
4. Require quarterly public DHS reporting on the docket, releases and declined detainers.

## Sources

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**

Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026 | Draft for editorial review; copy deadline Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026

## Executive summary

- ICE's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories as of July 21, 2024. The non-detained docket alone held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide and 15,811 convicted of sexual assault, plus another 222,141 awaiting criminal charges.
- Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.
- From October 2020 through July 2024, state and local law enforcement agencies declined 23,591 ICE detainers, and in 2,897 of those cases ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject.

## 1. Thirteen Thousand Convicted Killers ICE Does Not Hold

On Sept. 25, 2024, then-acting ICE Director Patrick J. Lechleitner answered a request from Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, with numbers no briefing book could soften. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories. Of those, 425,431 convicted criminals sat on the non-detained docket, the ledger of cases in which ICE holds no one.

How should the country size the public-safety cost of illegal immigration? Begin with the question no agency has volunteered to answer: of the people on the federal government's immigration ledger, how many have killed someone? ICE's answer of July 21, 2024, was 13,099 for homicide convictions alone, and the offense list runs on from there.

The offense categories are the point. The non-detained docket that day included 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault. Another 222,141 people on the same docket were awaiting criminal charges, 1,845 of them on murder charges.

These are adjudicated criminal convictions in the files of the agency Congress charges with removing criminal aliens from the United States. They are not projections, and they are not advocacy. ICE did not report how many of the 13,099 are finishing sentences in state or county custody and how many are already in the community. Either answer indicts the status quo. A convicted killer finishing a state sentence walks out the prison gate into the country unless a federal detainer is honored. A convicted killer already in the community is a federal warrant that has not been served.

The docket has grown under administrations of both parties: 368,574 convicted criminals as of August 2016, 405,786 as of June 2021 and 425,431 as of July 2024, roughly 15% more in eight years. What stands between that docket and the public is bed space Congress funds and local cooperation Congress has never required.

## 2. One in Three Federal Sentences

The federal courts quantify the flow. In fiscal 2024 the U.S. Sentencing Commission reported 61,678 sentenced cases, and 21,304 of them involved noncitizens, 34.7% of all individuals sentenced. Nearly nine in 10 of those noncitizens, 88.7%, were illegal aliens; another 8.5% were legal aliens.

The immigration guideline was the most common basis for a noncitizen sentence, at 72.3%, followed by drug trafficking at 17.6%. A September 2024 GAO review found the same pattern over a longer window: about three-quarters of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023, 76%, had an immigration offense as their most serious conviction.

Nor is the caseload an abstraction. The Sentencing Commission's profile of the fiscal 2024 noncitizen defendant: 94.4% men, an average age of 38, and 65.9% Mexican nationals, followed by Honduras at 8.7% and Guatemala at 5.8%.

Federal figures are a floor, not a ceiling. Homicide, rape, robbery and assault are prosecuted overwhelmingly in state courts, and a noncitizen convicted in a state courthouse never appears in the Sentencing Commission's files. The federal data that do exist describe a criminal-alien caseload the government already cannot finish.

## 3. Texas Puts a Number on It

Texas is the one state that records immigration status in its criminal conviction files, which makes Texas Department of Public Safety records the country's best available record of how often illegal aliens are convicted of crimes. An analysis of those conviction records by the Center for Immigration Studies concludes that illegal aliens are convicted of crimes in Texas at higher rates than native-born Americans, because prior studies counted only illegal aliens identified at intake and missed illegal aliens identified as such only after incarceration.

No other state keeps these records. For the other 49, neither Congress nor DHS can say how many of a state's convicts are illegal aliens, which is reason enough to write the reporting requirement into federal law.

The deeper lesson is about denominators: every claim that illegal-alien crime is trivial rests on denominators that understate the offending population. When Congress legislates on the strength of crime-rate claims, it should demand the underlying records, not the summary.

## 4. The Detainer Problem: 23,591 Refusals

Interior enforcement fails at a single, identifiable point: the transfer of custody. ICE's own letter to Congress describes jurisdictions that refuse to honor "ICE detainer requests, even for noncitizens who have been convicted of serious felonies and pose an ongoing threat to public safety." From Oct. 1, 2020, through July 22, 2024, state and local agencies declined 23,591 detainers, and another 1,205 were lifted because ICE received insufficient notice. In 2,897 declined cases, ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject. ICE's Detainer Acceptance Tracker, current as of June 21, 2024, lists 551 institutions that do not accept immigration detainers at all and another 146 that accept them only in limited fashion.

The cost of refusal is not hypothetical. On Feb. 22, 2024, Laken Riley, 22, a nursing student at Augusta University, was killed while running on the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Jose Ibarra, a 26-year-old Venezuelan national, had entered the country illegally near El Paso in September 2022 and been released pending his immigration case. He was arrested in New York in August 2023 on a child endangerment charge and released before ICE could file a detainer, and he was wanted in Georgia for missing a court date in a shoplifting case. In November 2024 an Athens judge convicted him of Riley's murder and sentenced him to life without parole.

Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act (Public Law 119-1, signed Jan. 29, 2025), which requires the Department of Homeland Security to take into custody aliens charged with theft. The law closed one gap. Detainer compliance, bed space and public reporting close the rest.

## Recommendations

1. **Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention capacity, and direct ICE to take custody of every noncitizen on the non-detained docket convicted of homicide or a violent felony on the day other custody ends.
2. **Condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance.** Require state and local grantees to honor ICE detainers and comply with 8 U.S.C. 1373, and withhold discretionary funds from agencies ICE lists as noncompliant.
3. **Expand Section 287(g) nationwide.** Fund new delegation agreements in every state, prioritizing jurisdictions where detainers are declined and criminal aliens are released.
4. **Publish the docket.** Require DHS to report quarterly on the size of the non-detained docket, releases by criminal category and every declined detainer, by agency.

The federal government already knows who these offenders are; it compiled the docket. What it has not done is take custody, require cooperation and publish the numbers until Congress makes it. The data in this brief are the government's own. The choice about what to do with them belongs to Congress.

*Data appendix and sourcing for every figure in this brief: "Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, Data Appendix," Founders' Square Institute, October 2026.*

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14: Fact Sheet

**Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show**
By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.
Draft for editorial review | Publication date: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026

## Key statistics

**1. 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide sat on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.** Another 15,811 on the same docket were convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 of assault. [1]

**2. 425,431 convicted criminals in all were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.** The national docket carried 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories, and another 222,141 on the non-detained docket were awaiting criminal charges. [1]

**3. Noncitizens were 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024: 21,304 of the 61,678 cases reported.** [2]

**4. 88.7% of those sentenced noncitizens were illegal aliens.** Another 8.5% were legal aliens. [2]

**5. 72.3% of noncitizen federal sentences in fiscal 2024 were under the immigration guideline.** Drug trafficking was next at 17.6%. Across fiscal 2018 to fiscal 2023, 76% of federally sentenced noncitizens had an immigration offense as their most serious conviction. [2][3]

**6. State and local agencies declined 23,591 ICE detainers between Oct. 1, 2020, and July 22, 2024.** In 2,897 of those cases ICE later had to re-apprehend the same subject. [1]

**7. 551 institutions refuse ICE detainers outright.** Another 146 accept detainers only in limited fashion, under ICE's own Detainer Acceptance Tracker, as of June 21, 2024. [4]

**8. The convicted-criminal non-detained docket grew from 368,574 in August 2016 to 425,431 in July 2024, about 15%.** It passed 405,786 in June 2021. [1][5][6]

## What Congress should do

1. Fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, with mandatory ICE custody for homicide and violent-felony convictions at the end of other custody.
2. Condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance and compliance with 8 U.S.C. 1373.
3. Expand Section 287(g) agreements nationwide.
4. Require quarterly public DHS reporting on the docket, releases and declined detainers.

## FSI Brief: 13,099 Noncitizens Convicted of Homicide Sit on ICE's Non-Detained Docket

**New data brief urges Congress to fund custody, require detainer compliance and publish the docket**

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026: The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy Brett Kessler.

ICE's Sept. 25, 2024, letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, showed 662,566 noncitizens with criminal histories on the agency's national docket as of July 21, 2024. The non-detained docket alone held 425,431 convicted criminals, including 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide, 15,811 convicted of sexual assault and 62,231 convicted of assault, with another 222,141 awaiting criminal charges.

Federal sentencing records point the same way. Noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of all individuals sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024, 21,304 people, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.

The brief also documents 23,591 detainers declined by state and local agencies between October 2020 and July 2024, 2,897 of them subjects ICE later re-apprehended, and closes with the murder of Augusta University nursing student Laken Riley in Athens, Georgia, in February 2024.

"Every number in this brief is the federal government's own," Kessler said. "ICE counted 13,099 noncitizens convicted of homicide on a docket of cases it does not hold, and the Sentencing Commission found that one in three people sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024 was a noncitizen. Congress does not need more anecdotes to act on interior enforcement. It needs to fund custody, require detainer compliance and publish the docket."

The brief recommends four steps for Congress: fund custody for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, condition federal law enforcement funds on detainer compliance, expand Section 287(g) agreements and require quarterly public DHS reporting.

Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a Hill fact sheet are available from the institute; Kessler is available for interviews.
